> they have root on your box

Or they have your discarded dead drive from your backup disk that you forgot to enable full disk encryption on. Or they rooted a machine that you were using "ssh -A" on to forward your agent, and have been able to temporarily hijack your SSH agent session. Or there's an information disclosure vulnerability in your web browser that allows them to read files from your hard drive, though without control of what files they can read, and by chance the attacker got lucky and one of the files was .ssh/id_rsa.

While the above description goes way further than I probably would, and yeah, 2FA would be more reasonable, there are good reasons to practice defense in depth, and try to design systems that have a chance of staying secure even if one of your assumptions fails like "private key is compromised".

comment_text.value:
keeping track of which keys have been added to your local ssh-agent is a tedious task. SSH is very promiscuous when it comes to using SSH keys, and once you make use of another key it will happily add that to your current agent session.

I've only found this to be true with gnome-keyring's ssh-agent emulation (which isn't complete last time I checked, since it doesn't support -c) and the ssh-agent that OSX's keychain provides. They implicitly show keys added if they have known filenames in ~/.ssh (id_rsa, for example) in the output of `ssh-add -l`. To make matters worse, decrypting the key file puts the passphrase in the key chain, so even if you put as password on your ssh key, it's still accessible after you login and authenticate to the keychain service.

The ssh-agent that is distributed with openssh does not do this and requires keys to be added explicitly.

Both scenarios you mentioned would, I believe, benefit from using keychain (see below).

Let's suppose I have an account tests@host which runs the tests (scripts) that need to login to an array of machines.

In order for keychain to be helpful here, you need two prerequisites.

1) You need to be able to interactively login to tests@host once after bootup; after that you don't need to touch the machine again.

2) Then, the test scripts need to say

    . $HOME/.keychain/$HOSTNAME-sh
once before executing any ssh command (the line above simply imports the ssh-agent session variables into the current environment).

edit: I removed the Nagios references as other posters rightly point out that there are more endemic ways to collect information with Nagios.

comment_text.value:
I built SLCR to address known limitations in spec-driven development. Specs codify a project's desired behavior in a human-optimized format that serves as a central source of truth for implementation agents. But when agents re-ingest the entire document when implementing, or translating to tickets it can introduce errors in different ways:

1. Ingesting the entire spec can lead to context bloat, which not only costs extra tokens, but also decreases agent coherence. 2. Translating spec to tickets can be lossy because agents may make small omissions or conflate information required across multiple tickets. Further, errors compound from agent session to session, making small omissions or missed details early in the process much bigger problems after multiple rounds of iteration.

SLCR (Sliceable, Linked, Checkable Requirements, pronounced slicer) is a new open-standard document format to make sure agents build to spec every time, without sacrificing human readability. Requirements live in one structured spec file (TOML, JSON, or YAML), with typed edges between requirements forming a DAG. Agents read small, task-specific walks of the DAG called slices, which provide them with all of the context they need to understand a given requirement with none of the superfluous context.

Requirements can have acceptance criteria that can be checked by a validators, which is a mapping to an executable tool to verify the requirement, vitest, your linter, or ast-grep. Requirements can be composed with AND, OR, or XOR, and the SLCR CLI can check whether each requirement is satisfied, so your spec is always synced to your codebase's current status. This helps prevent multi-session agent drift and misalignment by ensuring that no agent session invalidates existing pinned requirements.

A slice is one requirement plus the context it actually needs, determined by walking the DAG from a leaf node back to the root. When an agent picks up a ticket, you give it the slice instead of the whole spec, eliminating superfluous text unrelated to the requirement at hand. People still get the full picture, because the CLI renders the whole spec to deterministic, read-only Markdown. There's also an agent skill that teaches agents to use the CLI and write valid SLCR.

This tool is for engineers and tech leads on long-lived codebases who are giving agents real implementation work and want a check beyond reading the diff. If you're writing one-off scripts or throwaway prototypes, you probably don't need this.

The format is an open standard. The reference implementation written in Rust and released under the MIT license. Pull requests welcome!

Repo: https://www.github.com/wack/slcr Site: https://www.slcr.dev

comment_text.value:
I would like to offer an alternative view here. I have about 10 years of experience as an attorney doing mostly dispute resolution (voluntarily left the bar in 2016 IIRC), and 10+ as a software dev.

It seems to me that many people believe that the primary benefit that attorneys can receive from AI is searching through droves of statutes and/or court decisions. This is certainly part of the job, especially in common law countries. But regardless of the legal system, much more substantial gains can be had elsewhere in practical day to day work. It is not often an experienced attorney needs AI to explain law to them, especially if you're working in a field you specialize in. But in almost all cases, at least in dispute resolution, an attorney would benefit a lot from an AI agent going over the matter documents to highlight stuff like this:

- possible contradictions between the opposing party's arguments now and their arguments let's say 4 years ago when they filed their statement of claim (in long running cases often parties' positions will drift over time)

- possible misalignment between the opposing party's own evidence and their arguments that depend on said evidence

- potential problems with representation, for example an important notice being signed by a person that now is a management board member, but back then did not formally have the right to represent the company

Many disputes in court are at the end of the day decided by small or not-so-small issues like these. Before AI what attorneys did was to just sit down and try to read the matter materials are thoroughly as possible. This was of course an imperfect solution. Now with AI much of this can be handed off to a machine. AI is especially good at these types of needle-in-a-haystack tasks. So in other words, in my opinion lawyers do not benefit so much from AI having an inch deep view of the whole world, but rather benefits from a mile deep view of the specific matter at hand.

Due to this I believe that law firms do not need custom LLMs, the frontier ones today are good enough for such tasks. And I also believe law firms do not need custom harnesses. Again, the ones from frontier labs fit very well already. What law firms need in practice, in my opionion, is this:

1. strict context management - for each agent session the attorney should be able to not just limit the agent to a project, but to specific files or folders inside that project, often the unit "project" is not granular engouh (think a project containing emails from the client to the attorney where they describe what "really happened" - this text should never be accessible to AI unless the attorney specifically wants it to)

2. strict agent isolation - by default a law firm should start AI agent sessions in VMs that have no internet access (other than to the AI provider and whitelisted sites) and no file system access to the machine it runs on

If these 2 requirement are effectively met, I do not see a reason why law firms would need anything legal-specific in their AI setup. Harvey and Legora provide a one-stop solution. But they also provide vendor lock-in. In a couple of years I think the natural next step for most larger law firms is self-hosted AI once prices come down to a more reasonable level. So I would encourage firms to already today try to make decisions that will likely make this transition easier in the near future.

Take all of the above with a grain of salt. I am the founder of liitmik.com (isolated AI agents for law firms), so I have a skin in the game.

I find their post to be a little light on details, but my read is that they're essentially doing what you're complaining they should.

They're mapping the identity back to "agent" instead of "person". With the optional ability for the agent to present an "agent:person" combo in cases where it was triggered by a person.

Some quotes that imply but don't actually technically clarify what I mean:

> we now had a way to treat each cloud agent session as its own identity

> Once the human approves, access is scoped to the cloud agent session ID and the specific database that was requested.

> Using OIDC, cloud agents can request and be approved for short-lived access as they would with databases above. Requests are always logged in Formal and attributed to both the cloud agent and the engineer that launched it.

It sounds like they're not just attesting that the agent is the person, they're always scoping to a new combined identity.

So there's no confusion over whether it was a person, an agent, or an agent started by a person. (however where you go from there for culpability is a different question...)

But it doesn't seem like there's a case where a person did a thing (with their own credentials) and can then point a finger at an agent as say "oh it went rogue".

comment_text.value:
I think there are certain parts of certain products where the implementation details are really important, or where you need to make sure the behavior is fully reviewed/understood, or some invariant maintained. In some places that's the entire job and in other places almost none of it.

If you're running tons of product/UX experiments code review is just going to waste everybody's time. But the volume of changes you can make now is so large, someone could touch something important about at any given time without proper oversight.

IMO an effective team has to be able to either trust each other enough/be accountable enough that code review is mostly unnecessary, or everybody just works really independently on mostly separable things, or you regularly pair/mob-program.

If you can trust your colleagues not to pump out code without messing it all up or turning everything into slop, or creating large amounts of work for other people, things are great. Realistically most dev teams have a wide range of skills and personalities and people also make mistakes, and code review helps us build shared knowledge and collaborate.

Maybe there is too much of a moral hazard from the reviewer's role as a cosigner, or some people are only as conscientious as necessary to get things done (not a problem writing every line by hand)... but people can ruin code review for everyone else by demanding an asymmetric level of accountability/judgment and oversight.

The bigger issue for me is whether or not you still do code review, you need to build shared knowledge within teams. I really think we should be reviewing our colleagues' coding agent session logs

Not even to critique them (but that could be useful), but just to understand what it is they are actually trying to do/what mental model they're operating under, and if there are issue in the PR, what miscommunication or technique or process could help fix it? I think a lot of people feel that asking to see those logs is invasive or embarrassing, but the problem is that it's just really hard to build a model for how someone works or thinks without it. You don't need that in a deontological sense, but you do if you want to fix coordination problems.

comment_text.value:
In general, in my experience, grep is better than almost anything else you can use. It's very very fast and efficient, very flexible, and does not require any indexing pass, is never out of date, and doesn't require you to guess ahead of time what files you might want to search or how to process search tokens.

"Search your files, repos and agent sessions, locally, and give your agents the best context for the job. One search points them to the few passages that matter, instead of grepping the whole disk."

Grep is already searching for relevant passages with a single tool call. This is clearly LLM written copy. It makes literally no sense.

This reminds me of the dating app advert I keep seeing on tiktok, which says that other dating sites "force you to be the loudest voice on your profile". There's no interpretation that makes sense, it's just the typical LLM gibberish.

Indexing local files makes search faster (in theory, but in practice maybe not for less than a few tens of GB of local files on fast SSD), but not more flexible or requiring less tool calls.

It also will always suffer from being a little behind the on disk state, which is terrible when you are trying to do something like find all the references to something under active development, or when changing branches. Consider you checkout a branch and call this tool, it will just lie to you, telling your LLM there are matches in files that no longer match, getting line numbers wrong, missing matches in other files. Every time you change branches it will go nuts trying to reindex everything. The best case scenario is still probably performance on par with grep but out of date and doing a ton of extra work to index files whether or not you ever need to search them.

Grep can take general regex, which more or less can't be indexed, so there's very few things that are more flexible or produce less tool calls than grep.

Grep is also absurdly fast, if you don't know how fast it is it's faster than you think. Here I use ripgrep to search every piece of code I have checked out, around 11GB of data (more or less) in 0.2s (regular gnu grep takes 4s, mostly because it doesn't exclude .git/ folders and only uses one processor):

  xyz@xx:~% du -sh checkout
  11G checkout
  xyz@xx:~% time rg robotic checkout|wc -l
  19
  rg robotic checkout  1.14s user 1.07s system 1151% cpu 0.192 total
  wc -l  0.00s user 0.00s system 1% cpu 0.192 total

comment_text.value:
I don't know if you've noticed, but when Claude Code, Codex, or any other agent needs to find code, it runs grep. It searches your files for an exact string, reads a few results, and greps again until it finds what it wants. You pay tokens and wait for every round.

That worked fine when repos were small. But codebases are growing fast, partly because agents now write so much of the code. Every grep round costs more than it did last month, whether you notice it or not.

There's a second problem: grep only finds what you already know how to name. Ask it for "where we handle rate limits from the billing provider" and it gets 0% right on the first try, because it needs the exact string.

So I built Pensieve. It's a local index of your code, documents, and past agent sessions. Any agent can query it over MCP and get the few files that matter on the first try. A few cents saved per lookup doesn't sound like much. It adds up over hundreds of lookups a day.

Check out Pensieve!

Your other comment is flagged as dead so I'll reply here:

> I like the idea of using a “local inbox for agent sessions” because switching between different contexts can be more frustrating than the actual time it takes the agent to run.

> But I’m curious about how you see the inbox being useful beyond simply storing and replaying conversations.

> A few things would help me understand the practical value:

> What does a session actually contain? Is it just the conversation, or does it also include things like prompts, code changes, test results, Git commits, and other context? Can you reliably replay a session? Ideally, someone should be able to see what task was given, what the agent changed, what tests were run, and whether the task actually passed. What happens when work gets interrupted? If I pause one task and start another, can I come back later without losing the context or putting the project into a confusing state? How do you prove the work was completed? For example, can the system show the tests that were run, the changes made, and whether they passed? How is everything kept safe? If everything runs locally, that's great, but I'd still want to know how filesystem, network access, and logs are controlled.

> Even a small example showing something like how long it takes to go from starting a task to getting a working result, compared with the current workflow, would make the benefits much easier to understand.

---

Thanks for the questions! I like your suggestion about providing a small example. I'll put that together. Email me at matt@alcubi.ai and I will send it to you when it's ready. In the meantime, this page from the documentation may help to provide some of the details you're looking for https://alcubi.ai/delegator/docs/dev/concepts/ticket-lifecyc...

A session includes the scoped task request (ticket) and the code changes that are made on a separate git branch in a new worktree. You can enter the agent session at anytime with the "dg chat" command. That will allow you to look into the details of how the agent accomplished its work. So even though the runs execute in the background, the agent session is always available if you want to jump into it. I'll use this command when something was unclear to ask for follow-up changes. The agent will still have all the context in its session from the work it previously did so there's no extra context loading needed in these case.

If works gets interrupted, the ticket status moves to the Failed inbox. You'll see that clearly from the output of the "dg" command which shows the various inboxes. When this happens I'll use "dg chat" to attach to the agent session to understand what went wrong. Usually, this is something like the Claude/Codex API being down. When the API is back up, I run "dg restart" to restart the processing from where it left off. Since all work is done in separate branches and worktrees there's no ability for your project's main branch to be left in a confusing state.

The agents will run your test suite that's setup. delegator is just the orchestration layer. You can customize any steps you'd like the agents to follow via your AGENTS.md file. That will be taken into account when the agents run. So for example, you could add in your AGENTS.md file that for any delegator ticket they work on to include details in the commit of tests that were run. It's very flexible like that so you can customize it for your setup.

For safety, I've gotten to the point where I trust that agents are only accessing data that they need so there are currently no guardrails in place. This is something you could add to your AGENTS.md file to get information about but that's not deterministic. I could add in features to support this. Please email me at my email above to let me know a bit more about what you'd like to see and I can work on that.

Hope this helps and thanks for taking a look!

My GPUS are Rtx3090s with 24GB ram. You guessed correctly.

I do not enjoy the fact those cards cost more than their msrp 6 years later, but there is a much more important consideration than money (which also makes sense, but about that later). It is the fact soon people will not be able to do my job without AI at all. Even now if I didn't use it I think I'd be out competed very quickly.

And having the ability to run it locally, using a really useful, not toy model is very useful. It makes you independent from Anthropic deciding to ban your account for example.

As for money, it is an open secret the biggest cost of coding agents use is input tokens not generation. I tend to use about 1.3B input tokens per week on claude code with only 7-8M out. Out if this 80% is cached. And the cache is pretty restrictive. You have 5min cache and 1h cache. If you don't keep reading over that time your cache expires on the cloud. Then your 500k context counts as 500k input in its entirety.

And the numbers I mentioned would cost thousands of USD a week at API prices.

But when you control inference, you can keep your cache for as long as you want and save it to disk.

I tend to have up to 10 coding agent sessions open at a time. Some are used once a week. I never use more than 5 at the same moment. Having 15 full contexts cached in RAM basically moves my local cache utilisation to 95%+

Basically I think the AI companies will soon require us to pay the real price for the inference. I prefer to be ready.

comment_text.value:
I work on AI tooling at QA Wolf and I recently wrote this post.

Everyone is giving agents their own sandboxes these days, so that part isn't new. But I wanted to share the "why" and what we learned from building them. We first built them the way you build anything else in the cloud, but agent sessions don't behave like cloud jobs and a lot of cloud habits were wrong for them.

A few examples:

1. We first built a microservice that was responsible for managing each agent session, and thought we could scale it horizontally. That doesn't work, not if you want to give your agents a real file system and tools that need to be installed on that machine. We later gave each machine its own sandbox.

2. Our agents power our UI, but also live in Slack, Github threads and wait for people to reply. Our sandboxes had a 1-minute timeout and a cold-start. So once a sandbox died, it took anywhere from 10 to 30 seconds to spawn, because of which the users had to wait longer before they received a response from our AI on the UI or in the threads. Now, we maintain warm pools of sandboxes which can be acquired by a session in milliseconds and each sandbox is kept alive for 5 minutes after each reply.

The post is fairly high level, but if you want more detail on any part of it, I'm happy to talk about it here.

This tracks with what I've observed, as a fan-and-sometimes-user. They look to be funding a skunk works - which started with their version of Cursor (Jules or something), which wasn't great.

They are working on a cli agent; I tried it, but it silently injected hooks into all my other cli agents to re-target JB inference APIs, which caused me to burn through my JB tokens in like two minutes and b0rked all my running agent sessions.

They are working on a spec-driven thing, which I attempted to try but getting burned by the cli thing I abandoned it. It looks really interesting - it's a meta-harness, built and shipped with one of the Spec-Something frameworks, where you define your own specs for your projects, kinda like snake-eating-it-own-tail-of-specs. If spec-driven is The Future, they are at least trying.

There have been a few other things I can't recall, but my observation is that they are taking generative AI seriously as an existential threat, and probably (as another poster here put it) "heating the office burning tokens".
